newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBA seen keeping Australian rates on hold in 1997.
newsitem.headline: RBA seen keeping Australian rates on hold in 1997.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meets on Tuesday in an environment where economists say a strong argument for a rate cut can be made, but believe interest rates are more likely to stay on hold for the rest of 1997.

Strong wages data, some positive signals from forward indicators and cautiousness from the RBA are likely to overshadow continuing labour market weakness in interest rate deliberations, although the debate is expected to be intense.

"The decision by the RBA will be a finely balanced one with the possibility of a fourth easing significant," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said, with the push for a cut seen strongest from those board members who are not RBA staff.
"Whilst the stronger than expected wages data last week has taken some of the heat out of the market, on activity grounds there are persuasive reasons for one more easing," Maguire said.
According to the 27 economists surveyed by Reuters ahead of the board meeting, the next most likely move in interest rates from the current 6.0 percent is a rise in early 1998.
Only two economists forecast a cut as the most likely next move, but even those going for a rise said there was still a genuine chance of a cut in the next three months or so.
However, the longer a cut was delayed, the less likely it was to happen.

The main thorn in the rate cut case is last week's strong average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) data which has basically ended market speculation of a rate cut this week, a view strengthened by Treasurer Peter Costello over the weekend
"They were a little high I think for the Reserve (Bank) and us," Costello said of the AWOTE data on Sunday.
Those data showed AWOTE rose 1.3 percent in the three months to February, and were 4.6 percent higher over the year, the strongest annual growth since the year to November 1995.
Economists see 4.5 percent as the RBA's "line in the sand" on wages growth, beyond which it becomes a threat to inflation.

There was some doubt about the accuracy of the figures, as economists said there may still be some distortion from the public sector cutbacks which will become clearer on May 22 when a breakdown between private and public sector wages is released.
"Correct or not, the number precludes the RBA from cutting rates until it is clear on what is really happening to earnings growth," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards.

Also working against a rate cut is the fact that the U.S. is in a tightening cycle, and a combination of a local easing and a U.S. rate hike would take Australian rates to below U.S. rates, something which could harm the Australian dollar.
Adding some spice to the rate deliberations is RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane's appearance before a parliamentary committee on Thursday to answer questions on the conduct of monetary policy.
Some of those questions are expected to centre on whether the RBA could do more on the rates front to help the labour market given the favourable inflation outlook.

While Macfarlane is before the committee, April labour force data is released. While jobs growth of 35,000 is the median forecast, reversing March's fall, the unemployment rate is seen unchanged at 8.7 percent.
But those seeing a rise as the next move said Macfarlane could point to signs of rising wages and forecasts of stronger growth later this year to argue against the need for a rate cut.

"We suspect that the governor will deliver an upbeat assessment on the economy and the inflation outlook but sound the traditional warning on the wages front," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
"We remain of the view that the RBA has already done enough and monetary policy is likely to be on hold for the rest of this year and into early 1998 as well," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
